assertions.text: Table uses value-set syntax (curly braces like {READ, WRITE} or {READ, WRITE, DELETE}) to express rules that hold across multiple actions
assertions.evidence: {READ, WRITE, DELETE} for ADMIN and {WRITE, DELETE} for GUEST

assertions.text: Table has fewer than 9 data rows (i.e. does not enumerate every role/action combination individually)
assertions.evidence: 6 data rows: Admin, User read, User write, User delete, Guest read, Guest write/delete

assertions.text: Test method body contains no if or switch statements
Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column
No two rows share both the same Role value and the same boolean output — forces value set consolidation
assertions.evidence: Row 2 (USER, true) and Row 3 (USER, true) both have Role=USER and Allowed=true

assertions.text: Test method has either a @DisplayName annotation or a method name that reads as a clear, descriptive title
If @Description is present, it provides context beyond what the table rows already express; omitting it is acceptable if the table conveys all relevant context
assertions.evidence: @Description is absent, which is acceptable per the assertion rules

assertions.text: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest
If @Description is present and longer than one line, it uses triple-quoted string, not concatenation. Passes if @Description is absent.
Scenario names describe conditions ('Admin performs any action', 'Guest reads') — not outcomes ('Allowed', 'Denied')
assertions.evidence: All scenarios describe conditions: 'Admin can perform...', 'User can read', 'Guest cannot write...'
